title: Two ways to be wrong
objectives: Tell type I from type II errors, and trade one against the other.

screens.prose: A trading signal fires today. Either it has a real edge, or it is noise. You either trade it or ignore it. The table holds the four ways the day can go.
screens.question: Tap the two cells where your decision is a mistake.

hints.text: Read each cell as a pair: what the truth was, and what you did.
One mistake is in the Trade it row, and one is in the Ignore it row.
Trading with no edge is a mistake. So is ignoring a real edge. Tap those two cells.

feedback.correct: Trading on noise and ignoring a real edge are the two mistakes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In each cell, ask whether the decision matches the truth.

byKey.diagonal: You tapped the two right decisions. Trading a real edge and ignoring noise both match the truth.
byKey.r0c2: You tapped trading a real edge. That decision matches the truth, so it is right.
byKey.r1c1: You tapped ignoring noise. There was nothing to trade, so ignoring it is right.
byKey.r0c1: You missed trading on noise. A trade with no edge behind it is a mistake.
byKey.r1c2: You missed ignoring a real edge. Walking away from a real edge is a mistake too.

explain.text: The mistakes sit off the diagonal. Trading on noise is one kind of error; missing a real edge is the other. Every test risks both.

screens.prose: Now the signal is a test statistic $z$. With no edge ($H_0$), $z$ follows the left curve. With a real edge ($H_1$), it follows the right one. We trade when $z$ is past the cut-off. Drag the cut-off and watch both shaded areas.

derive.caption: Cut-off {{fixed(c, 3)}}: trade on noise {{fixed(values.alpha, 3)}}, miss the edge {{fixed(values.beta, 3)}}

screens.question: As the cut-off moves right, what happens to the two shaded areas?

options.text: The $H_0$ area shrinks and the $H_1$ area grows

options.why: You watched only the right tail. The shaded part of $H_1$ is left of the cut-off, so it grows.
The $H_0$ area is the tail past the cut-off. Moving right leaves less of that tail.

options.text: The $H_0$ area grows and the $H_1$ area shrinks
options.why: You have the directions swapped. Move the cut-off right and read the caption again.

feedback.correct: Fewer trades on noise, more missed edges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the cut-off to 3 and compare the caption with 1.645.

explain.text: Moving the cut-off right means trading less often. You trade on noise less, so the $H_0$ tail shrinks. You also miss more real edges, so the $H_1$ area grows.

screens.prose: Trading on noise is a **type I error**: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true. Its chance is $\alpha = P(\text{reject} \mid H_0)$. Missing a real edge is a **type II error**: keeping $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true. Its chance is $\beta = P(\text{do not reject} \mid H_1)$.
screens.question: With the cut-off at 1.645, fill in the chance of each decision under each truth.

hints.text: Read $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from the caption, then place them.
Under $H_0$ you either reject or you do not, so each column adds to 1.
Column $H_0$: 0.05 and 0.95. Column $H_1$: $\beta = 0.196$ at the bottom, so rejecting has chance $1 - 0.196 = 0.804$.

feedback.correct: Each column adds to 1, and the errors sit off the diagonal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each column is one truth, so each column adds to 1.

byKey.r0c1: Rejecting under $H_0$ is the type I error. Its chance is $\alpha$, the $H_0$ tail past the cut-off.
byKey.r1c1: Under $H_0$ you either reject or you do not. Take $\alpha$ from 1; the rows need not add to 1.
byKey.r0c2: Under $H_1$ rejecting and not rejecting add to 1. Take $\beta$ from 1.
byKey.r1c2: Not rejecting under $H_1$ is the type II error. Its chance is $\beta$, the $H_1$ area left of the cut-off.

explain.text: Each column is one world, so its two chances add to 1. The off-diagonal cells are the errors: $\alpha = 0.050$ and $\beta = 0.196$. The diagonal cells are the chances of getting it right.

screens.prose: A risk manager says: never trade on noise, so make $\alpha = 0$. The cut-off moves to the far right, and the test never rejects.
screens.question: If the edge is real, what is the chance this test misses it?

options.why: You counted only trading on noise. A test that never rejects also never catches a real edge.
That was $\beta$ at a cut-off of 1.645. Moving the cut-off right made $\beta$ grow.

options.text: 0.5: it is a coin toss now
options.why: Nothing is random about a test that never rejects. Under $H_1$ it fails every time.

hints.text: If the test never rejects, what does it do when the edge is real?
Look at how much of the $H_1$ curve is left of the cut-off.
All of the $H_1$ curve is left of the cut-off. The test always keeps $H_0$, so $\beta = 1$.

feedback.correct: With $\alpha = 0$ the test never rejects, so $\beta = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the test does when the edge is real.

explain.text: A test that never rejects has $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 1$. Removing one error entirely buys the other in full. Every useful test accepts some of each.

screens.prose: The desk will accept missing a real edge 10% of the time. Find the cut-off that gives exactly that, and see what it does to $\alpha$.
screens.question: Set the cut-off so that $\beta = 0.10$.

hints.text: Which way does the cut-off move to make $\beta$ smaller?
$\beta$ is the $H_1$ area left of the cut-off. Moving left shrinks it.
Slide left from 1.645 and watch the caption. $\beta$ reaches 0.10 near 1.22.

feedback.correct: Near 1.22, $\beta = 0.10$ and $\alpha$ has risen to about 0.11.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch $\beta$ in the caption and stop when it reads 0.100.

byKey.too-high: $\beta$ is still above 0.10 there. Move the cut-off further left.
byKey.too-low: You went past it: $\beta$ is below 0.10, and $\alpha$ grew more than it had to.

explain.text: To cut $\beta$ from 0.196 to 0.10 you moved the cut-off left, to about 1.22. That raised $\alpha$ from 0.05 to 0.11. One error fell only because the other rose.

screens.prose: The desk tightens the test to $\alpha = 0.01$, so the cut-off is 2.326. With a real edge, $z$ is normal with mean 2.5 and sd 1. Useful values: $\Phi(-0.174) = 0.431$ and $\Phi(0.174) = 0.569$.
screens.question: What is $\beta$ now?

hints.text: $\beta$ is the chance $z$ lands at or below the cut-off when $H_1$ is true.
Under $H_1$, $z - 2.5$ is standard normal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the cut-off by the $H_1$ mean, then use $\Phi$.

byKey.power: 0.569 is the part of $H_1$ past the cut-off. That is the chance of catching the edge, not missing it.
byKey.alpha: 0.01 is $\alpha$, the error under $H_0$. $\beta$ is measured under $H_1$.
byKey.old: 0.196 was $\beta$ at the old cut-off of 1.645. The cut-off has moved right.

explain.text: Under $H_1$, $P(z \le 2.326) = \Phi(2.326 - 2.5) = \Phi(-0.174) = 0.431$. Cutting $\alpha$ from 0.05 to 0.01 more than doubled $\beta$, from 0.196 to 0.431.

screens.prose: A quant runs this 5% test on 1,000 signals. From experience, 100 have a real edge and 900 are noise. The test catches 80% of the real edges.
screens.question: What share of the 1,000 decisions are mistakes?

hints.text: The 5% is a chance given $H_0$. Which signals does it apply to?
Type I errors sit in the noise column, type II errors in the real-edge column.
Noise traded: $0.05 \times 900 = 45$. Real edges missed: $0.2 \times 100 = 20$. Add them and divide by 1,000.

feedback.correct: 45 trades on noise plus 20 missed edges: 65 mistakes in 1,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the mistakes in each column, then divide by 1,000.

byKey.five: You took 5% as the error rate on every signal. It is a chance given $H_0$, so it applies only to the 900 noise signals.
byKey.only-type-one: You counted the 45 trades on noise but not the 20 real edges the test missed.
byKey.only-type-two: You counted the 20 missed edges but not the 45 trades on noise.
byKey.share-of-trades: You found the share of trades that are noise, 45 of 125. The question asks about all 1,000 decisions.

explain.text: The 5% applies only inside the noise column: $0.05 \times 900 = 45$. In the real column the test misses $0.2 \times 100 = 20$. The overall 6.5% depends on how many signals are real, just as in the base-rates lesson of Conditional Probability.

screens.prose: You found both errors as areas. With cut-off $c$, and $z$ centred at $m$ under $H_1$: $$\alpha = P(z > c \mid H_0) = 1 - \Phi(c), \qquad \beta = P(z \le c \mid H_1) = \Phi(c - m).$$ Raising $c$ lowers $\alpha$ and raises $\beta$.
screens.question: Which expression is $1 - \beta$, the chance of catching a real edge?

options.why: That is $\beta$ itself, the chance of missing the edge.
That is $\alpha$, worked out under $H_0$. Catching the edge happens under $H_1$.
That is the chance of keeping $H_0$ when it is true. It says nothing about $H_1$.

feedback.correct: Under $H_1$ the test either rejects or it does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Under $H_1$, the chances of rejecting and not rejecting add to 1.

explain.text: Under $H_1$ the test rejects with chance $1 - \beta = 1 - \Phi(c - m)$. With $c = 1.645$ and $m = 2.5$ that is 0.804. The next lesson names it and asks how to raise it.

screens.prose: We derive $\beta$ for the cut-off rule. Under $H_1$ the statistic is $z = m + Z$, where $Z$ is standard normal.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\beta = P(\text{do not reject} \mid H_1)$: the definition
$\beta = P(z \le c \mid H_1)$: we keep $H_0$ exactly when $z$ is at or below the cut-off
$\beta = P(m + Z \le c)$: under $H_1$, $z = m + Z$
$\beta = P(Z \le c - m)$: subtract $m$ from both sides
$\beta = \Phi(c - m)$: $\Phi$ is the standard normal cdf

hints.text: Start from what $\beta$ means in words.
The decision rule turns the words into an inequality on $z$.
Definition, then the rule $z \le c$, then substitute $z = m + Z$, subtract $m$, and name the cdf.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line rewrites the one before it.

byKey.s1: The definition comes first: every other line rewrites it.
byKey.s2: The rule $z \le c$ turns the definition into an event, so it comes second.
byKey.s3: Substituting $z = m + Z$ needs the event on $z$ first.
byKey.s4: Subtracting $m$ needs $m + Z$ on the left first.
byKey.s5: Naming $\Phi$ needs a standard normal on the left, so it comes last.

explain.text: Each line rewrites the event, so the chance stays the same. The trick is line 3: under $H_1$ the statistic is the standard normal shifted by $m$. Then $\beta$ is one lookup of $\Phi$.

screens.prose: A bank's fraud model tests $H_0$: the payment is genuine. A false alarm costs £4 of staff time; a missed fraud costs £250. Of 10,000 payments, 20 are fraud. The model has two settings.
screens.question: Which setting has the lower expected cost per 10,000 payments?

options.text: A: a missed fraud costs over 60 times a false alarm
options.why: You compared the cost of one error of each kind. There are 9,980 genuine payments to raise alarms on, and only 20 frauds to miss.
You added $\alpha$ and $\beta$. B's sum, 0.44, is larger than A's 0.25, and the sum ignores the costs and the counts.
You swapped the two totals. Work out each setting's false alarms and missed frauds again.

hints.text: Expected cost adds up two parts: false alarms on genuine payments, and missed frauds.
There are 9,980 genuine payments and 20 frauds.
A: $0.05 \times 9{,}980 \times 4 + 0.20 \times 20 \times 250$. B: $0.01 \times 9{,}980 \times 4 + 0.43 \times 20 \times 250$.

feedback.correct: B wins: false alarms on 9,980 genuine payments dominate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the cost of each setting's false alarms and missed frauds.

explain.text: A costs £1,996 in false alarms plus £1,000 in missed fraud: £2,996. B costs £399.20 plus £2,150: £2,549.20. Which error costs more depends on the price of each and how often each truth occurs.

ideas: A test can be wrong in two ways: rejecting a true $H_0$ (type I) or keeping a false one (type II).
$\alpha = P(\text{reject} \mid H_0)$ and $\beta = P(\text{do not reject} \mid H_1)$. Moving the cut-off trades one against the other.
Which error matters more depends on what each costs and how often each truth occurs.

formula.name: The two error rates
formula.note: For a one-sided $z$ test with cut-off $c$, where $z$ is centred at $m$ under $H_1$.

summary.trap: A 5% test is not wrong 5% of the time. The 5% is a chance given $H_0$; the overall error rate depends on how many nulls are true.

quiz.prose: A risk model tests $H_0$: this book is within its limits. One book is in fact over its limit, and the model does not flag it.
quiz.question: Which error has the model made?

options.why: A type I error flags a book that is fine. Here a bad book went unflagged.

options.text: No error: it kept $H_0$, which is the default
options.why: Keeping $H_0$ is an error when $H_0$ is false, and here it was false.
One decision on one book can make only one error. Here the false $H_0$ was kept.

feedback.correct: A false $H_0$ was kept: type II.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which hypothesis was true and what the model decided.

explain.text: The truth was $H_1$: the book is over its limit. The model kept $H_0$, so this is a type II error. A risk model's misses are often the costlier error.

quiz.prose: A trading signal is traded only when its $z$ statistic passes a cut-off. The desk raises the cut-off from 2 to 3.
quiz.question: What does that do to the two errors?

options.text: Fewer trades on noise, more missed moves
Both kinds of error become rarer
options.why: You moved only one error. A stricter cut-off also lets more real moves through untraded.

options.text: More trades on noise, fewer missed moves
options.why: A higher cut-off means trading less often, so trades on noise get rarer, not commoner.

options.text: Nothing, the test is the same
options.why: The cut-off is part of the test. Moving it changes both $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A higher cut-off means trading less often.

explain.text: Raising the cut-off shrinks the $H_0$ tail past it, so $\alpha$ falls. More of the $H_1$ curve now sits below the cut-off, so $\beta$ rises.

quiz.prose: A one-sided test rejects when $z > 1.645$. Under $H_1$, $z$ is normal with mean 3 and sd 1. Useful values: $\Phi(1.355) = 0.912$ and $\Phi(-1.355) = 0.088$.
quiz.question: What is $\beta$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\beta$ is the chance under $H_1$ of landing at or below 1.645.

byKey.power: 0.912 is the chance of rejecting under $H_1$, which is $1 - \beta$.

explain.text: $\beta = P(z \le 1.645 \mid H_1) = \Phi(1.645 - 3) = \Phi(-1.355) = 0.088$. The further $H_1$ sits from the cut-off, the smaller $\beta$.

quiz.prose: A team tests 200 strategies at $\alpha = 0.05$. Only 20 have a real edge, and the test catches half of those.
quiz.question: What share of the 200 decisions are mistakes?

feedback.correct: 9 trades on noise plus 10 missed edges: 19 of 200.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each kind of mistake in its own group, then add.

byKey.five: You took 5% as the overall error rate. It applies only to the 180 strategies with no edge.
byKey.type1: You counted the 9 false passes but not the 10 real edges the test missed.

explain.text: Type I: $0.05 \times 180 = 9$. Type II: $0.5 \times 20 = 10$. That is 19 of 200, or 9.5%, nearly twice the 5% headline.
